metadata.title: Post-Closing Integration: A Plan, or a Tracker?
metadata.purpose: Answer what a team should build the day an M&A deal closes: a one-time integration plan, or a live phased tracker. Lands the carry-out that you can't manage an integration you're not tracking -- the tracker has to outlast the plan.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible integration-tracking account from the one real phrase the source did contain ('post-closing M&A integration tracker -- phased workplan') rather than lifting facts that were never written.

beats.narration_text: Someone whose deal just closed asks: do we need a master plan for after closing? Wrong tool. A plan freezes one moment; integration moves. What they need is a tracker. Liam, in for Bear.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Do we need a plan for after the deal closes?', hesitates on 'plan', corrects to 'tracker', lands the real question

props.text:

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('plan' -> 'tracker') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A plan is one document -- written the day the deal closes, listing what has to happen. It optimizes for clarity in that one moment. What it sacrifices: visibility the day after. Workstreams start moving in parallel -- IT, HR, finance, contracts -- and a static document can't tell you which ones are on schedule and which have quietly stalled. This works if you value a signed record; it fails if you need to know where the work is right now. A live tracker fixes what a plan gives up.

shot.new_visual_element: A sealed 'plan' document card listing named workstreams; a fourth, unlabeled workstream sliding in beneath it, unmarked and unlit

production_viz.label: A plan only lists what's named on day one
production_viz.mechanic: A card labelled 'INTEGRATION PLAN' with a wax-seal glyph and three named workstream chips inside it, fully lit. A fourth chip slides in from below the card, dim and unlit, passing underneath without touching the plan card. A caption fades in beneath: 'the plan never knew it existed.'

beats.narration_text: Here's the mechanism. Every workstream on the tracker takes four fields: task, owner, target phase -- day-one, day-thirty, day-one-hundred -- and today's status. Four fields, no more. That constraint is the design choice: enough shape to catch a missing owner, few enough to actually fill in. Watch the anchor. The vendor-contract workstream is marked day-thirty on the org chart, with no owner ever assigned to it. Held up against the four-field shape, the gap is visible on sight.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- four field chips lighting in turn (task / owner / phase / status), then a dim, unlabeled workstream card set off to the side

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- four fields, then the unowned workstream
production_viz.mechanic: Four chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a field (task / owner / phase / status), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A single card appears off to the side, dim and outlined only, reading 'vendor contracts -- day 30' with no owner field filled in -- visibly incomplete against the four-field shape just shown. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: That workstream gets the same four fields as everything else -- owner assigned, phase set, status tracked -- and now it's visible instead of silently late. Now name the limits. 'In progress' is not the same as 'on schedule'; status is a snapshot, not a guarantee. And a fully staffed tracker on day one doesn't mean nothing else surfaces -- new workstreams turn up as integration proceeds. The tracker reveals gaps. It does not close them.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the dim card lighting up with all four fields filled and sliding into the main tracker; then split into 'tracked is not on schedule' and 'staffed is not complete'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- tracked, not cleared
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIM CARD RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in one field at a time (task / owner / phase / status) until fully lit, then slides into a row alongside other tracked workstreams. It splits into two cards: left reads 'status: in progress' with a struck-through 'ON SCHEDULE' beneath it labelled 'tracked is not on schedule'; right reads 'tracker: staffed today' with a faint new unlabeled card appearing at its edge labelled 'staffed is not complete'.

beats.narration_text: You can't manage an integration you're not tracking. Build the phased tracker, not a single plan. The plan holds for day one; the tracker outlasts it.

props.sparkLine: Tracker first. The plan only holds for day one.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt to read with me. List the workstreams for a hypothetical post-closing integration -- IT systems, HR and benefits, finance consolidation, vendor contracts. For each one, assign an owner and a target phase: day-one, day-thirty, or day-one-hundred. Mark today's status. Any workstream with no owner is the gap the tracker just found -- which is the point.

props.command: List the workstreams for a hypothetical post-closing integration -- IT systems, HR and benefits, finance consolidation, vendor contracts. For each one, assign an owner and a target phase: day-one, day-thirty, or day-one-hundred. Mark today's status.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. It asks the model to build you a phased integration tracker with four fields per workstream -- task, owner, target phase, status -- and to flag every row where the owner is still generic instead of a real name. Go deeper: which workstream is most likely to surface after day one instead of showing up on day one, and what signal should you watch to catch it early?

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm the ops lead for a company we just acquired -- the deal closed yesterday. Build me a phased integration tracker, not a static plan. Return a table with one row per workstream. Include IT systems, HR and benefits, finance consolidation, vendor contracts, and any workstream you would add. For each row give me four columns: task, owner role, target phase (day-one, day-thirty, or day-one-hundred), and a default status of 'not started'. Then, in a second table below, flag every row where the owner is still a generic role instead of a real name -- those are the gaps I need to close first.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: which workstream in that tracker is most likely to surface after day one instead of appearing on day one, and what early signal would tell me it's coming?
